questions.scenario: You have finished a feature that adds idempotency, reformats every file in the package, and renames several classes. The diff is 2,300 lines.
questions.question: What is the best way to submit it for review?
options: Submit it with the description 'various improvements'
Merge it directly because the tests pass
Submit one PR and ask reviewers to focus on the important parts
Split it: a formatting-only PR, a rename/refactor PR, then a focused behaviour PR with a full description and test evidence
questions.explanation: Reviewers catch far more in small, single-purpose changes. Separating mechanical changes from behaviour changes lets each be reviewed at the right depth.

questions.scenario: While reviewing, you notice that a new endpoint GET /api/v1/statements/{id} checks the CUSTOMER role but not that the statement belongs to the caller.
questions.question: How should you comment?
options: Rewrite the code yourself and push to their branch without discussion
Leave a nit asking for a comment in the code
Mark it blocking, explain the risk (another customer's statement can be read by changing the ID), and suggest an ownership check with a negative test
Approve and mention it in the team chat later
questions.explanation: A broken object-level authorisation check is a security defect that must be fixed before merge. A clear explanation and a concrete suggestion make the fix fast.

questions.scenario: A reviewer writes: 'This is badly written.'
questions.question: Which rewrite is a better review comment?
options: "I would never do it this way."
"Please fix."
"You always write long methods."
"suggestion: this 80-line method mixes validation, fee calculation and persistence; extracting calculateFee() would make the tier rules easier to test. What do you think?"
questions.explanation: Good comments address the code, explain why, propose a concrete change and signal their importance. Comments about the person or with no direction do not help.

questions.scenario: You are preparing a PR that changes how transfer fees are rounded.
questions.question: What should the PR description include? (Choose two.)
options: The full source code pasted into the description
How it was tested, including boundary cases, and any rollout or migration risks
Why the change is needed (for example the incident or requirement) and the new rounding policy
A list of every file name changed
questions.explanation: Reviewers need context (why), the approach, test evidence and risks. The diff already shows the code and files.

questions.scenario: A reviewer asks you to change a loop to a stream. You think the loop is clearer for this case.
questions.question: What is a professional response?
options: Ignore the comment and merge
Change it without comment even though you disagree, then complain elsewhere
Escalate to your manager
Reply with your reasoning; if it is marked as a nit or suggestion, it is your call, and if the team disagrees, accept their decision
questions.explanation: Optional suggestions leave the decision to the author, and disagreements are resolved with reasons. Silent merges and escalation over style damage team trust.

questions.scenario: A bank's change-management policy requires that every production change is approved by someone other than its author.
questions.question: Which repository setting enforces this?
options: Allowing administrators to bypass reviews
A CONTRIBUTING.md file asking people to get reviews
Branch protection on main requiring at least one approving review (from CODEOWNERS where relevant) and passing status checks
Requiring signed commits only
questions.explanation: Branch protection with required reviews makes the four-eyes principle a technical control rather than a request.

questions.scenario: Before requesting review, you open your own PR's diff on GitHub.
questions.question: Which of these should you remove or fix during self-review?
options: The tests, to make the diff smaller
Nothing; reviewers will find everything
Debug log lines, commented-out code and unrelated changes, and make sure CI is green
The PR description
questions.explanation: Self-review catches noise and obvious problems, so reviewers can spend their attention on design, correctness and risk.
